USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Enter the G20 meeting with Xi prepared to trade a pause on the scheduled January 1, 2019 escalation (List 3 from 10% to 25%, and the threatened ~$267B in additional tariffs) for concrete Chinese commitments — verifiable purchases of US goods (soybeans, LNG) and enforceable structural reforms. Keep the tariff threat on the table as leverage, but do not let the talks collapse and do not trigger the January escalation, which would deepen the market selloff and intensify farm-belt political damage. Signal willingness to delay the January increase in exchange for a real package, as the administration is already weighing.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to US interests is real but not existential (threat_score +0.25). We hold the initiative — Section 301 tariffs cover ~$250B of Chinese imports and China has had to retaliate (timeline: List 1/2 at 25%, List 3 at 10% on 2018-09-24). But the escalation is now costing us through two channels. First, markets: the S&P corrected ~10% and the Dow turned negative for 2018 with FAANG in a bear market, October the worst month since 2011, driven substantially by trade-war fears (web: Reuters 2018-10-29, CNBC 2018-11-20); Baa corporate yields widened to 5.28% and WTI collapsed from ~$75 to ~$51, flagging a growth scare in the macro data. Second, domestic politics: China's retaliation on soybeans hurt the farm belt and anti-tariff Democrats gained farm-district seats in the November midterms (web: Forbes/Guardian). The US economy itself remains strong (industrial production up, CPI contained near 0.5% over window), and we retain clear leverage — so this is not high threat. That leverage is precisely why negotiate (action_score +0.1) is right rather than escalating: pushing to 25% on January 1 plus $267B in new tariffs would compound market and farm-belt pain and hand Xi a rationale to walk, while a pause-for-concessions deal (reportedly under internal consideration, per NYT 2018-11-27) converts our bargaining position into gains and stabilizes both markets and the political base. Firm but deal-seeking — not unilateral concession — is the correct stance at the summit.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Go into the G20 Buenos Aires meeting with Xi at the table and a genuinely constructive posture: signal willingness to offer concrete, face-saving concessions — lifting retaliatory tariffs on US soybeans and LNG and committing to increased purchases — in exchange for deferring the January 1 escalation of List 3 from 10% to 25% and halting the further $260B+ tariff threat. Do not escalate; the higher-stakes sequence (25% on $200B plus a possible additional $260B) is the cliff we cannot afford to trigger, and the imminent summit is our best available off-ramp. Hold firm on matters that touch CCP legitimacy (permanent structural reform, abandoning industrial policy), but be ready to negotiate seriously this week.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is high but not existential. Evidence drives this reading: US Section 301 coverage on ~$250B of our exports is already live (List 1 $34B @25% July 6, List 2 $16B @25% Aug 23, List 3 $200B @10% Sep 24), and the escalation to 25% is scheduled for Jan 1 — the single largest cliff (event_timeline). The real economy is already feeling it: Q3 GDP slowed to 6.5% (slowest since 2009), October retail sales grew just 8.6% (weakest since May, an explicit 'consumption downgrade'), October new lending collapsed to ~half of September, and fiscal revenue fell 3.1% (SCMP, 14 Nov); FX reserves dropped $33.9B in October to an 18-month low with the yuan near the 7.0 level after seven straight monthly losses (Reuters/SCMP, 7 Nov). This sits squarely at the +0.5 'high' anchor (major export sectors hit, FX pressure, firm-level targeting such as ZTE and threatened Huawei), and I place it slightly higher at +0.6 because the Jan 1 escalation and the additional $260B+ tariff threat hang directly over us at the decision date. However, this is not existential (+1.0): reserves remain ample (~$3T), capital controls contain outflows, and we retain leverage through US farm imports. On action, escalation would be self-defeating: retaliating further risks triggering the full $267B new-tariff tranche Pence/Lighthizer are pushing and an economic cold war. The knowable facts show an off-ramp: Trump is under market pressure (Dow ~9% off its October 3 high after the House midterm flip, GM layoffs) and his moderates (Kudlow, Mnuchin) are urging a truce that defers the Jan 1 hike in return for concrete Chinese commitments (NYT, 28 Nov; WaPo, 27 Nov). That means negotiation, offering limited creditable concessions, is the disciplined move — action_score +0.2 (moderate de-escalation lean into talks), action_level 'negotiate' — because it buys off the worst outcome without conceding on structural/legitimacy lines.
